background.definition: Myocardial infarction is evidence of myocardial necrosis in a patient with evidence of decreased perfusion from coronary artery disease (CAD).

list.listitem: 1.3 million patients are admitted to hospital with unstable angina/non-ST-elevation MI (UA/NSTEMI) and 350,000 with ST elevation MI (STEMI) in the United States every year.
Between 2.1% and 6.1% of the population have coronary heart disease, depending largely on geographic and socioeconomic factors.
CAD is projected to cost an estimated $151.6 billion in direct and indirect costs in 2007 in the United States.
Complete or partial occlusion of a coronary artery by: Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque (type 1 MI). Imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand (type 2 MI).
An acute coronary syndrome is usually caused by plaque rupture from nonobstructive but vulnerable plaques.

The vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque has a rich lipid core, a thin fibrous cap, many T lymphocytes, and fewer smooth muscle cells. When the plaque ruptures it exposes the thrombogenic subendothelial basement membrane to the circulation, which is followed by acute thrombosis, coronary occlusion, and myocardial necrosis.

Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is commonly caused by advanced atherosclerotic plaque with thrombosis that is not occlusive and may be associated with increased myocardial demand.
Coronary vasospasm may worsen the coronary occlusion.
See chapter on CAD for guidance regarding screening and primary prevention.
Absolute smoking cessation and avoidance of second-hand smoke.
Control blood pressure to less than 140/90 or 130/80 if diabetic.
Treatment with a high potency statin.
Reduce intake of saturated fats and trans-fatty acids; increase fiber and omega-3 fatty acids in diet.
Exercise for at least 30 minutes every day.
Keep body mass index between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m2.
Start aspirin 75 to 162 mg/d and continue indefinitely in all patients unless contraindicated.

Start and continue clopidogrel 75 mg/d in combination with aspirin for at least 6 months after percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent (and 12 months for the newest generation of stents) and at least 1 month for bare metal stents. The exact timing of discontinuation of clopidogrel is still controversial. Recent studies suggest that prolonged therapy with clopidogrel after the minimum duration does not reduce cardiovascular events but can have higher costs and increased bleeding.

Start and continue ACE inhibitors in all patients with ejection fraction (EF) less than 40% and consider in all other patients. May use angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) if patient is ACE inhibitor intolerant.

The traditional recommendation has been to start and continue a beta-blocker in all patients.However, a collaborative analysis of several large RCTs in patients with acute MI and normal ejection fraction (5 trials with 17,801 participants compared beta-blocker with placebo in this population. At baseline, the groups were similar with a mean age of 62 years, 45% having ST elevation MI, and 94.5% getting a percutaneous coronary intervention. The most commonly used beta-blockers were bisoprolol (47%) and metoprolol (46%). After 4 years there was no difference for the primary composite outcome of all-cause mortality, AMI, or heart failure (8.1% with beta-blocker, 8.3% without).

A French study randomized 3698 patients who had survived an acute MI at least 6 months earlier and who were currently taking a beta-blocker. Those with heart failure or an ejection fraction less than 40%, a recent CV event, or had another indication for beta-blockers were excluded. Participants were randomized to either discontinue the beta-blocker or to continue taking the same drug at the same dose. The study showed reduced hospitalizations with continued use of a beta-blocker after AMI, but no change in CV death, AMI, or stroke. There were no differences in reported quality of life between the groups.
There is inconclusive evidence to support continuing or stopping estrogen therapies after acute MI.
Anti-inflammatory therapy canakinumab was associated with lower rate of recurrent MI in subjects with a CRP level >2mg/L.
Lipid lowering therapy with anacetripib was associated with a lower rate of recurrent MI compared to statin therapy alone.
Lipid lowering therapy with evolucamab was associated with a lower rate of recurrent MI compared to statin therapy alone.
Patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) typically have prolonged substernal chest pain radiating to the shoulder, arms, or jaw. C
Order a stat ECG on all patients with suspected AMI. A
Order serial cardiac enzymes (CK-MB and highly sensitive troponin I or T) in patients with suspected AMI and normal ECG. A
The presence of elevated cardiac enzymes associated with clinical or ECG evidence of ischemia is diagnostic for MI. A

list.listitem:
Detection of rise and/or fall of cardiac biomarkers (preferably troponin) with at least one of the following:
Symptoms of ischemia. The severity of pain on a numeric scale is not predictive of outcomes. ECG changes indicative of new ischemia (new ST-T changes or new left bundle branch block (LBBB). Development of pathologic Q waves on the ECG. Imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality.

Classically "acute coronary syndrome" includes both ST elevation MI (STEMI) and non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI). A clinical classification of Type 1 through Type 5 AMI is summarized below:
Type 1 (spontaneous MI): event due to rupture of atherosclerotic plaque, ulceration, erosion, dissection or fissuring resulting in an intraluminal thrombus and myocardial necrosis. Type 2 (MI secondary to ischemic imbalance): something other than plaque leads to an imbalance between myocardial demand and supply, such as hypotension, endothelial dysfunction and coronary vasospasm. Type 3 (cardiac death due to MI): persons who suffer a cardiac death with symptoms and ECG findings suggestive of MI but without elevated biomarkers. Type 4 and 5 (MI associated with revascularization procedures): injury or infarction occurring during a cardiac procedure.

The classic clinical presentation of MI is characterized by chest pain (crushing, substernal, pressure-like, exertional, or same as previous pain diagnosed as MI), duration more than 20 minutes, with radiation to the jaw, neck, shoulder(s), or arm(s).

Symptoms that most strongly rule in AMI when present include radiation to both arms, radiation to the left arm or right shoulder, and a third heart sound. Findings that best rule out MI include pleuritic chest pain, sharp or stabbing chest pain, positional chest pain, and pain reproduced by palpation. Symptoms are more predictive for younger patients (age 30-64 years) than for those years or older. If clinical suspicion for AMI is low, the presence of chest wall tenderness helps rule it out.

The Levine sign (a clenched fist held against the chest) has poor predictive value. In a series of 202 chest pain patients, only 11% had the Levine sign, and the predictive value was 50%; 20% were unable to describe their chest pain.

The presence or absence of cardiac risk factors is not helpful in determining whether an older person with chest pain has acute coronary syndrome; it is somewhat helpful among patients under age 40 (LR+ 7.4 for 4 or more risk factors).

Physical examination can be significant for jugular venous distention, S3 gallop, rales and pedal edema in heart failure; new or worsening holosystolic murmur in the mitral area due to acute mitral valve regurgitation; hypotension, tachycardia, cool and clammy extremities, and respiratory distress in cardiogenic shock; hypotension, clear lungs, elevated jugular venous pressure, Kussmaul's sign (attenuated drop in jugular venous pressure during inspiration), and prominent x descent in right ventricular infarction; and hypotension with a new harsh, loud holosystolic murmur heard at the lower left sternal border accompanied by a thrill in rupture of the interventricular septum.

Relief of chest pain with nitroglycerin is not useful diagnostically. In a study of 459 patients admitted with a diagnosis of "rule-out AMI," 31% received a final diagnosis of active CAD. Only 35% of these patients had pain relief with nitroglycerin, compared with 41% among patients without active CAD. At 4 months, clinical outcomes were similar in patients with and without chest pain with nitroglycerin.
Order ECG and serial cardiac biomarkers for all patients with suspected AMI.
ECG can show ST elevation or depression, new onset LBBB, pathologic Q waves, and/or new onset T-wave inversion.

The most commonly used cardiac biomarker is troponin I and T (obtained at baseline and 9-12 hours). Other cardiac enzymes include myoglobin (obtained within 3 hours of symptoms),and CK-MB isoenzyme (obtained at baseline and 3, 6, and 9-12 hours). CK-MB remains elevated for 24 to 36 hours, whereas troponin I and T are elevated for 7 and 14 days, respectively.

A negative standard troponin test 6 to 10 hours after the onset of chest pain in a patient without ischemic ECG changes makes the likelihood of cardiac death or MI very low in the subsequent year (1%).

The most accurate current tests are highly sensitive troponins (hs-TnI and hs-TnI), which can be useful as little as 2 to 3 hours following the onset of symptoms. A negative high sensitivity troponin T assay drawn at the time of presentation to the ED effectively rules out acute myocardial infarction, based on a systematic review of 23 studies. Using a cutoff of 14 ng/L as an abnormal test, the summary positive likelihood ratio was 3.9 and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.13, while for a cutoff of 3 to 5 ng/ml the LR+ was 1.7 and the LR− was 0.06. If the disease prevalence is 21%, typical in an ER setting, then one would miss two cases of acute MI by relying on the 14 ng/L cutoff, and less than 1 by relying on the 3 to 5 ng/L cutoff.

Echocardiogram can show wall motion changes, decreased left ventricular function in heart failure, and (less commonly) mitral regurgitation in posteromedial papillary muscle rupture and ventricular septal defect in rupture of interventricular septum.
Order emergent cardiac catheterization for STEMI and unstable NSTEMI patients.
An early invasive strategy (i.e., coronary arteriography within 72 hours of admission) is associated with improved outcomes.
LBBB, initial CK-MB elevation, and clinical impression of high risk are strong evidence in favor of AMI.

Cardiac MRI with gadolinium, dobutamine stress testing, late redistribution single-photon emission tomography thallium, and fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography scanning can all be used for viability testing after an acute coronary event.

The SCOT-HEART trial was a randomized trial in which 4146 adults with stable chest pain were randomized to receive usual care plus coronary computed tomographic angiogram (CCTA) or usual care alone. After 10 years, more adults who received usual care experienced a nonfatal myocardial infarction than those who were evaluated with CCTA (6.0% vs 4.3%; NNT = 61). There was no significant difference between groups in all-cause mortality or death from coronary heart disease.
Lee and colleagues have developed and extensively validated a rule to predict complications requiring ICU care that can be used to guide management decisions ().
The likelihood of normal left ventricular ejection fraction in patients with AMI can be predicted by a clinical rule.
Prognosis of patients with AMI can be predicted by the ACI-TIPI score, by a rule based on the initial ECG, or by a clinical rule based on data from the TIME II substudy.

The risk of AMI in patients with a normal or near-normal ECG can be predicted by a clinical rule and can identify patients at very low risk for AMI. The Goldman algorithm takes a stepwise approach to diagnosis of AMI.
Diagnostic scores based on the TIMI trial for STEMI () and NSTEMI have been developed and prospectively validated.
A variety of clinical rules (Kimmel, CADILLAC,Resnic,Bates, and Mayo) have been developed and validated to predict outcome of angioplasty.
See for a suggested approach to management of AMI.
Treat all patients with oxygen, pain control medications, and antiplatelet therapy including aspirin and heparin (or enoxaparin). A
Nitroglycerin may be given to relieve ischemic chest pain, except in patients with hypotension and right ventricular infarction. A
High-risk NSTEMI patients benefit from an early invasive strategy. A

Order emergent cardiac catheterization for all STEMI patients when door to balloon time is less than 90 minutes and for patients with cardiogenic shock; consider in patients with NSTEMI and severe heart failure and symptoms lasting more than 3 hours. A
Give thrombolysis within 30 minutes when percutaneous cardiac intervention (PCI) is not available or more than 90 minutes of delay is expected in door to balloon time. A
Refer patients with left main stenosis of more than 50% or triple-vessel disease for consideration of coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). B
Treat most patients post-AMI with aspirin or clopidogrel, beta-blockers, and statins (LDL target of 70-100 mg/dL) if no contraindications are noted.A
For patients with LVEF <40%, ACE-I therapy is indicated.

Cardiac catheterization is generally performed in suitable candidates with acute coronary syndromes. A meta-analysis failed to show significant difference in early versus delayed catheterization on patient outcomes.

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): PCI (or thrombolysis) is recommended by ACC/AHA guidelines (2025) for patients with STEMI. Specific guidance from ACC/AHA for PCI and urgent CABG follows:
STEMI presenting < 12 hours after symptom onset: primary PCI within 90 to 120 minutes. STEMI and cardiogrenic shock or hemodynamically unstable: CABG or PCI of culprit vessel regardless of time from symptom onset. STEMI presenting 12 to 24 hours after symptom onset: consider primary PCI. STEMI presenting > 24 hours: primary PCI is reasonable in patients with ongoing evidence of ischemia or life-threatening arrhythmia. STEMI presenting > 24 hours an no ischemia, arrhythmia or heart failure: do not perform primary PCI. STEMI and PCI not feasible or successful: If large amount of myocardium at risk consider urgent CABG. NSTEMI: revascularization recommended if intermediate or high risk of ischemic events (GRACE risk score 109 to 140 or > 140 points). If low risk NSTEMI then consider selective invasive strategy based on coronary CT angiography or stress testing.

Reperfusion therapy for STEMI: Give thrombolysis within 30 minutes of medical contact when primary PCI is not available or if a delay of more than 90 minutes in door to balloon time is expected. Thrombolysis is contraindicated in patients with hemorrhagic stroke, recent surgery, arterial or venous punctures and central venous line in noncompressible sites like the carotid, jugular, and subclavian, recent intubation, severe hypertension, and pregnancy. In the United States streptokinase, reteplase, alteplase (t-PA), and tenecteplase are currently available as thrombolytics. Thrombolysis reduces absolute mortality by over 50% when given less then 2 hours after presentation compared with both later thrombolysis and primary PCI.

Reperfusion at hospitals without PCI capability: STEMI and device activation <= 120 minutes or contraindication to fibrinolytic, transfer to hospital with PCI. STEMI < 12 hours and delay > 120 minute for PCI, give fibrinolytic therapy. STEMI 12 to 24 hours, transfer to hospital with PCI ST segment depression only (unless posterior MI suspected) do not give fibrinolytic therapy.
Oxygen: Current ACC/AHA guidelines (2025) only recommend supplemental oxygen when O2 saturation is < 90%.

Aspirin or clopidogrel: Give aspirin 162 to 325 mg at presentation and continue indefinitely thereafter for all patients without contraindications. Give clopidogrel to aspirin-sensitive patients. Aspirin decreases vascular mortality by 2.4% (NNT = 41). A pooled analysis of data for 28,982 patients from 7 RCTs with median 2.3 years follow-up found that the overall rate of major cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events was lower with clopidogrel than aspirin (2.6 vs 2.99 per 100 person-years; NNT=257) with no difference in the rate of major bleeding (0.71 vs 0.77 per 100 person-years). For the individual outcomes, clopidogrel was more effective than aspirin only for subsequent MI (0.99 vs 1.27 per 100 person-years; NNT = 358) and for stroke of any etiology (0.73 vs 0.88 per 100 person-years; NNT = 667).

P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor): An oral P2Y12 inhibitor should be given in addition to aspirin to patients with STEMI or NSTEMI as follows based on ACC/AHA guidelines (2025):
Percutaneous coronary intervention (STEMI or NSTEMI): aspirin + (ticagrelor or prasugrel). Cangrelor IV is a less well studied alternative. Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): aspirin + (ticagrelor or clopidogrel) No planned invasive intervention: aspirin + ticagrelor STEMI given fibrinolytic: aspirin + clopidogrel

Nitroglycerin: Nitroglycerin may be given to relieve ischemic chest pain except in patients with hypotension or right ventricular infarction, but does not improve clinical outcomes. Morphine is also indicated for pain relief (2 to 4 mg, repeating every 5 to 15 minutes, optionally using up to 10 mg).

Anticoagulation: Parenteral anticoagulation is recommended for all patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) by ACC/AHA 2025 guidelines:
NSTEMI: IV unfractionated heparin (UFH). If early invasive approach is not planned, enoxaparin or fundaparinux are alternatives to UFH. Patients undergoing CABG or PCI: continue parenteral anticoagulation until revascularization. Patienst with ACS undergoing PCI: IV UFH is recommended, with bivalirudin as an alternative. Consider IV enoxaparin (but not fondaparinux) at the time of PCI to reduce ischemic events. STEMI treated with fibrinolytics: continue parenteral anticoagulation for duration of hospitalization (up to 8 days) or until revascularization. For patients not planning on an invasive strategy, enoxaparin or fondaparinux are alternatives.

Beta-blockers: ACC/AHA guidelines recommend giving beta-blockers to all hemodynamically stable patients with AMI within 24 hours. Beta blocker use is associated with lower rates of hospitalization and revascularization in the year following acute myocardial infarction.

However, beta blockers may not have benefit in patients with a normal ejection fraction and no angina over the long term. A collaborative analysis of RCTs in patients with acute MI and normal ejection fraction (5 trials with 17,801 participants compared beta-blocker with placebo. The most commonly used beta-blockers were bisoprolol (47%) and metoprolol (46%). After 4 years there was no difference for the primary composite outcome of all-cause mortality, AMI, or heart failure (8.1% with beta-blocker, 8.3% without).

Statins: Continue or intensify high intensity statin therapy (defined as atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg) for all patients, including addition of ezetimibe if needed to achieve LDL-C < 70 mg/dl and ideally < 55 mg/dl.

Angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors: Give ACEIs to all patients within 24 hours after MI and ARBs to patients intolerant of ACEI. Long term therapy is determined by left ventricular function (i.e., for EF <40%). Consider a mineralicorticoid antagonist for patients with ACS, left ventricular ejection fraction < 40% who have heart failure symptoms and or diabetes mellitus.

Clopidogrel is added for at least 1 month after PCI with a bare metal stent and for at least 6 to 12 months after a drug-eluting stent.ACC/AHA guidelines (2021) recommend dual antiplatelet therapy for 1 to 3 months following PCI, with most patients discontinuing aspirin at that time. There is evidence that long-term clopidogrel therapy after stent placement is associated with more harm than benefit, and a recent FDA recommendation advocated considering ticagrelor or prasugrel.

Prolonged dual antiplalelet therapy (>12 months after AMI) with aspirin plus clopidogrel, prasugrel or tigagrelor may have benefit, but the NNT is modest (64 for recurrent MI and 220 patients for mortality benefit).

Adding ticagrelor to aspirin after myocardial infarction slightly lowers recurrent events (NNT = 83 over 3 years) but at an increased risk of bleeding. The overall clinical efficacy (including the cost of long term therapy) is less clear.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitor apixaban use after AMI is associated with excess bleeding without reducing ischemic events. Low-dose rivaroxaban reduces the rate of recurrent cardiovascular events when added to standard antiplatelet therapy. The role of these novel oral anticoagulants for routine use in acute coronary syndromes has not been well established.

Initiate high potency statins. Statin therapy intiated within 14 days of acute coronary syndromes reduces occurence of unstable angina at four months. Less evidence is availble suggesting a short term impact on mortality, recurrent MI, or stroke.
Adding ezetimibe to simvastatin further reduces cardiovascular events (NNT = 58 over 6 years), but it is not clear how this compares to high dose statin therapy (currently recommended by guidelines).
Insulin glargine therapy has not been shown to reduce major cardiovascular events or mortality in subjects with dysglycemia and cardiovascular disease (or risk factors).
Intensive glycemic control has likewise failed to demonstrate effects in reducing cardiovascular events versus conventional glyemic control in type 2 diabetes.

Evidence supporting specific therapy for type 2 MI (due to an imbalance in myocardial oxygen demand and supply) is lacking. A meta-regression analysis found a borderline correlation between PCI rate and in-hospital mortality at 1 year.
A polypill containing aspirin, high-intensity statin, and ACEi resulted in fewer cardiovascular events after myocardial infarction (NNT 31) versus usual care.
A trial randomized 7062 patients with AMI to colchicine, spironolactone, both or placebo and found no benefit after 3 years from either intervention.
ACC/AHA guideline (2025) recommendations for PCI in patients with STEMI are summarized above under "Drug therapy".

Primary PCI is the treatment of choice for STEMI when door to balloon time is less than 90 minutes, in patients with cardiogenic shock, and in patients with a high risk of bleeding. Even a small delay increases the risk of bad outcomes.Consider PCI in patients with severe heart failure and symptom duration of more than 3 hours. Revascularization of stenotic but non-culprit lesions is associated with a clinical benefit.

Primary PCI has the advantages of reduced reocclusion rate, good TIMI-3 flow rate, early risk stratification, reduced mortality, stroke, and reinfarction, reduced risk of intracranial hemorrhage, and shorter length of hospitalization. Use primary PCI with stents when coronary anatomy is favorable.
Routine thrombus aspiration at the time of PCI is not associated with decreasing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

A trial randomized 1163 patients with ST elevation MI to to complete revascularization with PCI guided by angiogrphy or by assessment of fractional flow reserve (FFR). There was no difference between groups in the composite of death from any cause, nonfatal MI, or unplanned hospitalization leading to urgent revascularization at 1 year (5.5% for FFR and 4.2% for angioplasty).

Patients 75 years or older with either ST-elevation or non-ST elevation MI have improved clinically important outcomes with complete, rather than culprit lesion-only, revascularization. This finding is similar to the findings in younger patients.
Patients with diabetes, left main stenosis greater than 50%, or triple-vessel disease should probably be referred for CABG but may be considered for PCI.

A study randomized patients 75 years and older with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (MI) to receive either invasive or conservative strategies. the early invasive strategy for older patients with acute non-ST elevation MI did not improve outcomes overall. Although there were significantly fewer nonfatal MIs with the early invasive strategy (11.7% vs 15.0%), there was no difference in all-cause mortality between groups, and the invasive strategy group had slightly more cardiovascular deaths (though this was not statistically significant).

Surgical revascularization does not improve mortality at 5 years in subjects with left ventricular dysfunction. Similarly myocardial viability measurements do not predict response to CABG. Surgical revascularization may reduce long-term mortality and recurrent myocardial infarctions in diabetic patients when compared to stenting.

The merits of PCI versus CABG in the short term depends on lesion location, but the long term comparison is still under study. Some data suggests less early myocardial infarction in patients with PCI, but more later deaths and myocardial infarction in patients treated with PCI rather than CABG.
A small RCT of 144 patients recruited within 72 hours of AMI found that coenzyme Q10 60 mg twice daily resulted in fewer cardiac events at 1 year (25% vs. 45%, NNT = 5).

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reduced the likelihood of death, nonfatal AMI, or nonfatal stroke after 3.5 years in a large study of patients with a recent AMI (NNT = 44).A meta-analysis of several studies, however, did not show a benefit for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. A subsequent randomized controlled trial failed to demonstrate benefit from n-3 fatty acid supplementation in subjects with dysglycemia.
Vitamin E is not helpful.Other multivitamins do not reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in men (including those with a history of cardiovascular disease).
Homocysteine-lowering agents sugh as B-complex vitamins have not shown a benefit in CAD.

In a large study of more than 21,000 older participants (aged 60 to 84 years), taking 60,000 IU vitamin D each month slightly reduced their likelihood of experiencing a major cardiovascular event (NNT = 172 over 5 years).
A randomized trial with 1000 patients with diabetes and a history of MI concluded that there was no benefit from EDTA chelation in reducing the risk of adverse cardiovascular events.
Cardiac rehabilitation is underutilized. It improves function and reduced hospitalization in older adults after MI.
Refer all ambulatory patients for cardiac rehabilitation.
Exercise combined with nutritional counseling has demonstrated a slowing of the atherosclerotic process and decreased rates of subsequent coronary events and hospitalization.
A Cochrane review concluded based on 24 rials with 3046 persons that home based cardiac rehab provides similar benefits to hospital or centre-based rehab.
Anxiety and depression are common in patients hospitalized for MI.
Psychological support and counseling during hospitalization can decrease anxiety and depression immediately and for up to 6 months after MI.
Treatment with cognitive-behavioral therapy and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors can be useful for patients with MI and depression that occurs in the year after the event.
A single RCT of 369 patients found that sertraline was safe and effective in patients following AMI.
Moderate coffee consumption appears to be safe after AMI.
A Mediterranean style diet is associated with positive outcomes in high risk subjects.
Oral contraceptives containing estrogens may slightly increase the risk of myocardial infarction or stroke, but the absolute increases are small.
Influenza vaccination is associated with lower cardiovascular mortality in patients with coronary artery disease.
Nonsteroidal use is associated with a higher risk of death after acute myocardial infarction (with the lowest increased risk seen with naprosyn).
Testosterone supplementation is associated with an increased risk of MI in elderly males.
A 3-day length of stay is reasonable for most patients with uncomplicated AMI. The cost of a fourth day is just over $100,000 per year of life saved.
A well-validated clinical algorithm can risk-stratify patients and guide the decision to admit to a standard hospital bed with telemetry or to the ICU (see ).
Elderly woman, diabetics, those with a history of MI and heart failure, and patients who did not receive reperfusion therapy are at higher risk of complications.

Cardiogenic shock: managed with intra-aortic balloon pump counterpulsation, positive inotropes (dobutamine and dopamine), and diuretics as needed. A Canadian trial randomized 192 patients with cardiogenic shock to milrinone or dobutamine and found no difference in outcomes.
Right ventricular infarction: managed with reperfusion and IV fluids. Avoid drugs that decrease right ventricular preload (diuretics, nitrates, and morphine).

Acute mitral valve regurgitation: caused by posteromedial papillary muscle dysfunction from underlying left ventricular ischemia and infarction. Treated with reperfusion and surgery in case of papillary muscle rupture.
Ventricular septal rupture: can be apical and simple or basal and complex. It is managed by surgical closure.
Rupture of left ventricular free wall: is almost always fatal and is managed with emergency surgery.

Ventricular tachcardia after MI: A trial randomized 424 patients with VT following MI to sotalol (or amiodarone) or catheter ablation. After 4.3 years follow-up, the primary outcome of death or ICD shock, VT storm or sustained VT occurred less often in the catheter ablation group (50.7% vs 60.6%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.75; 95% CI 0.58 - 0.97; NNT = 10. The primary advantage was from fewer episodes of treated sustained VT below the ICD detection limit (NNT = 8). Catheter ablation is a viable alternative to medical therapy for patients with a history of myocardial infarction and clinically significant VT.
Bleeding risk on antithrombotic therapies increases with concomitant nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs after acute MI.
A randomized trial of escitalopram versus placebo demonstrated a reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with prior myocardial infarction and depression.
Admit all patients to a monitored bed; admit high-risk or unstable patients to the CCU. Others may be admitted to telemetry or step-down unit.
Patients with STEMI who are stable should not be on bed rest for more than 12 to 24 hours.
Assess rhythm, heart rate, anginal symptoms, oxygen saturation, and fluid status frequently.
Abnormal serum potassium levels are associated with worse outcomes.
Mortality following hospital discharge for patients with untreated AMI is 10% in year 1 and approximately 5% each year after that. B
Patients treated promptly with adequate medical and interventional therapy have in-hospital mortality rates of 2% to 4% and 1-year mortality of 8% to 10%. A
TIMI risk score is useful in predicting outcome in both STEMI and NSTEMI. A
In studies before 1980, about 1 in 4 patients died before reaching the hospital, and 16% died in the hospital.
Mortality following hospital discharge for patients with untreated AMI is 10% in year 1 and approximately 5% each year after that.
Untreated, patients may die acutely from arrhythmias or subacutely from refractory heart failure.

A Danish study found that screening of asymptomatic people using coronary CTA will identify atherosclerosis in approximately 60% of men and 36% of women. A small proportion will have coronary artery partial obstruction. This group, as well as people with extensive atherosclerosis, regardless of level of obstruction, is at higher, but still low, risk of myocardial infarction (MI) over the next few years. Over a median follow-up of 3.5 years, 193 participants died due to any cause (2%) and 71 (0.7%) had a myocardial infarction (MI).
Troponin-T elevation and ST depression greater than 0.2 mV are associated with increased mortality and a greater risk of reinfarction rate over a 6-month period.

An initial ECG showing acute anterior infarction, right bundle branch block, left anterior and posterior hemiblock, atrial fibrillation or flutter, junctional rhythm, or prior AMI is associated with increased 30-day mortality. Failure to normalize ST segments within 1 hour of reperfusion is strongly associated with mortality (relative risk = 8.7).
Elevated brain natriuretic peptide (40 pg/mL) is also associated with increased 30-day mortality and congestive heart failure in MI.
Stress echocardiogram or myocardial perfusion scanning once acute coronary syndrome is ruled out may be helpful for clinical management if a non-invasive strategy is preferred.
Sudden death occurs in 1.4% of patients during the first month after AMI and in 0.14% per month for the next 2 years. It is more common in patients with lower EF.
Older, frail patients may not have different outcomes when considering invasive versus conservative management.
Follow-up periodically for risk factor modification and clinical assessment for optimal secondary prevention.
Perform exercise testing either in the hospital or early after discharge in STEMI patients not selected for cardiac catheterization and without high-risk features.
Use echocardiography in patients with STEMI to evaluate left ventricular function and suspected complications.
Diabetes is commonly diagnosed (31%) in the 3 months after initial presentation with AMI.
Home-based cardiac rehabilitation appears to be as effective as center-based programs.
See chapter on CAD for guidance regarding patient education.
Elderly patients have more complications but benefit equally from medical and interventional therapy after adjusting for comorbidities.
For elderly patients over 75 years, weigh early invasive therapy carefully in terms of functional and cognitive status.
If enoxaparin is used, adjust the dosage for those over 75.
MI during pregnancy is rare and is associated with poor outcome for the mother and fetus.
Atherosclerosis and spontaneous coronary dissection are the cause of most events.
In general, proceed with treatment as for nonpregnant patients.
Thrombolysis is relatively contraindicated in pregnancy.
Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy.

Patients get 1 point for each of the following risk factors: Age older than 65 years, three or more coronary artery disease risk factors, * severe angina within the past 24 hours, elevated cardiac enzymes, ST deviation of at least 0.05 mV, known coronary artery disease with ≥50% stenosis of at least one vessel. Aspirin use in the previous week, interpretation (all patients received enoxaparin). Abbreviations: AMI, acute myocardial infarction; STEMI, ST-elevation myocardial infarction; TIMI, Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (trial).*Family history, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking.
